rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The elution window will guide subsequent gradient trimming and selectivity tests.

Injection 1 already attained the maximum possible CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method while preserving the original as the maximum-score benchmark.

The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves the critical pair close to the resolution threshold. Increase temperature by one step to test whether selectivity improves while shortening retention further.

Higher temperature improved the critical middle pair, suggesting it may offset some resolution loss from a steeper gradient. Test a six-minute gradient at 55 C for a faster maximum-CRF method, while monitoring the narrowing first pair.

Narrow the solvent window to retain a slope close to the successful eight-minute gradient while reaching the elution region sooner. Use 50 C to balance improved middle-pair selectivity against the first-pair crowding observed at 55 C.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving its slope to shorten retention without strongly perturbing the critical middle pair. Check whether the first pair remains sufficiently retained and resolved at the higher starting organic fraction.
Slightly reduce gradient steepness to recover the middle pair’s resolution while retaining the faster starting window. This should offer a shorter fully resolved separation than injection 5.

Maximum CRF is already secured, so test a much steeper gradient for a potentially faster separation after the critical middle pair changes elution order. The lower temperature should help preserve separation of the early pair.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower slope to shorten the successful separation. Lower temperature should help protect the early pair from compression; the middle pair remains the main selectivity risk.

Use a shallower gradient and a modest temperature increase to recover the critical middle pair at the higher starting organic fraction. The endpoint remains comfortably above the observed elution window, reducing the risk of hold-phase retention.

Trim the endpoint and shorten the programmed gradient, giving a slightly steeper slope than injection 10. Its resolution margin may support a faster fully resolved separation, with the final peak still expected inside the gradient.

With maximum CRF secured, explore a distinct fast-separation regime using higher initial organic and lower temperature. This tests whether altered selectivity can resolve the middle pair under a short gradient while retaining enough separation among early peaks.

Probe whether a higher starting organic fraction and narrower window improve the fast regime’s middle-pair selectivity. This is exploratory: the first peak may remain essentially unretained, so early-pair resolution will also be checked carefully.

Halve the slope at the same starting composition and temperature to isolate the fast regime’s critical-pair response. The endpoint remains above the previous last-peak elution composition, so all six compounds should still elute promptly.

Further reduce the slope to test whether the critical pair can reach baseline resolution in the high-starting-organic regime. The final hold may delay the last peak somewhat, but the observed elution window suggests little risk of truncation.

The critical pair responds weakly to further slope reduction in this regime, so test a shifted solvent window instead. This may improve middle-pair selectivity and shorten the run, although compression of the first pair is a clear risk.

Test temperature selectivity at the high-organic setting where slope changes gave little improvement. Comparing directly with injection 14 will show whether warming can resolve the middle pair before the early pair becomes too compressed.

Return to the successful moderate-organic regime and test a slope between injections 6 and 7. This targets a slightly faster maximum-CRF separation, with the middle pair expected to lie close to the resolution threshold.

Test an intermediate starting composition with a shallower gradient, using lower temperature to preserve early-pair resolution. This probes whether the gap between the successful moderate-organic regime and the fast high-organic regime offers another fully resolved method.

Compare directly with injection 11 to measure temperature sensitivity at the fastest fully resolved setting. Cooling should improve the early pair’s margin; this run will establish whether the middle pair also retains full resolution.
Back off one endpoint step from injection 18 to restore the critical pair’s resolution. This targets a compact maximum-CRF method with more early-pair margin than injection 11.

Test whether a five-degree temperature increase can lift injection 18’s middle-pair resolution above 1.5 while shortening retention. The first pair may become limiting, so retain injection 11 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Test a small slope increase over injection 11 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary at 50 C. The middle pair may fall just below 1.5, but this grid point could shorten retention without the early-pair losses caused by higher temperature.

Refine the successful injection 5 into a shorter programmed gradient with a slightly shallower slope and an endpoint above the observed elution window. This should preserve maximum CRF while providing more early-pair resolution margin than injection 11.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower version of injection 21 for greater critical-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak well below 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
